samples.text:
The table shows the car ownership in one country in 1995, 2010 and 2025, and the two pie charts show how people go to work in 1995 and 2025.

In the table, the number of cars increased from 14.2 million in 1995 to 19.8 million in 2010 and then 22.1 million in 2025. The cars per 1,000 people also went up from 280 to 360 and after to 385. However, the percentage of households with no car decreased from 33% to 25% and then 23%.

In the pie charts, car was the most popular way to travel to work in both years, but it fell from 64% to 57%. Bus also fell from 14% to 8% and walking decreased from 12% to 8%. On the other hand, train increased from 6% to 10% and bicycle went up from 4% to 7%. In 2025 there was a new category, work from home, which was 10%.

Overall, car ownership increased over the period, but less people used car to go to work in 2025 and some people worked at home.
samples.why: Overview present but placed at the end and fairly general · all visuals covered accurately but mechanically · repetitive verbs (fell, increased) · errors with articles, tense and quantifiers that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The table provides data on car ownership in a country in 1995, 2010 and 2025, and the two pie charts compare the ways people commuted to work in the first and last of these years.

Overall, car ownership rose steadily over the thirty years. Despite this, the proportion of people driving to work fell slightly, while train travel, cycling and working from home became more common.

The number of cars grew from 14.2 million in 1995 to 19.8 million in 2010 and 22.1 million in 2025. Similarly, there were 280 cars per 1,000 people in 1995, but this figure had risen to 385 by 2025. Meanwhile, the share of households without a car dropped from a third to 23%, although most of this decline happened before 2010.

Regarding commuting, the car remained by far the most popular method, even though its share decreased from 64% to 57%. Bus use fell considerably, from 14% to 8%, and walking also became less common, falling from 12% to 8%. By contrast, the proportion of commuters taking the train rose from 6% to 10%, and cycling grew from 4% to 7%. In addition, 10% of people was working from home in 2025, a new category.
samples.why: Clear overview linking ownership and commuting · key changes highlighted, including timing of the decline · good range of linkers (Despite this, By contrast) · appropriate vocabulary · one or two minor grammatical slips.

samples.text:
The table sets out figures on car ownership in one country in 1995, 2010 and 2025, while the pie charts illustrate how people travelled to work in 1995 and 2025.

Although car ownership increased throughout the period, the car's dominance as a means of commuting weakened somewhat, with rail, cycling and home working all gaining ground.

The number of cars on the country's roads rose by almost 8 million over the thirty years, from 14.2 million to 22.1 million, with the sharpest growth occurring between 1995 and 2010. Car density followed the same pattern, increasing from 280 to 360 vehicles per 1,000 people in the first fifteen years but only to 385 by 2025. Correspondingly, the proportion of households without a car fell from 33% to 25% by 2010, before levelling off at 23%.

Turning to commuting, the car remained the principal mode of transport, although its share slipped from 64% to 57%. Bus travel and walking both declined, to 8% each, from 14% and 12% respectively. Train use, on the other hand, increased from 6% to 10%, and cycling from 4% to 7%. Perhaps most notably, working from home, which did not feature in 1995, accounted for 10% of workers by 2025.
samples.why: Concise overview capturing the central contrast · data grouped and compared skilfully across all three visuals · accurate figures · precise, varied vocabulary (density, levelling off, principal) · wide range of error-free structures.
